teaser: In 1338 Siena asked a painter what a well-run city looks like. He answered with a dance.
review_notes:
The image shows only the city half of the Effects of Good Government wall; the lesson says so.
Claim that the Nine lived inside the Palazzo Pubblico during their two-month term and could leave only on feast days: commonly reported, please confirm.
Claim that dancing in the streets was forbidden by Sienese statutes, and that the dancers may be men (scholarly hypothesis): please confirm wording.
Lorenzetti's death in the 1348 plague is traditional (he made his will that year); stated as probable.
Identification of small scenes (shoe shop, classroom, pack animals with wool bales, herdsman with sheep) follows the usual reading; the image is small for these details.
Wall length of about 14 m (46 ft) for the whole Effects of Good Government wall is approximate.

lesson.text: What does a well-run city look like? Not its laws or its speeches: its streets, on an ordinary morning. In 1338 the rulers of Siena put that question to a painter, and asked for the answer on the walls of the room where they met. Ambrogio Lorenzetti gave them shops, a school, a wedding and a dance.

The room is in the Palazzo Pubblico, Siena's town hall. Lorenzetti covered three of its walls in fresco, which means paint brushed onto fresh, wet plaster so that the color dries into the wall itself. One wall shows good government as a set of symbolic figures, one shows bad government, and the longest shows what good government produces. You are looking at the city half of that long wall.

Siena was run by nine citizens known simply as the Nine. Each team served for only two months, and during that time the men lived inside the town hall, away from their families and their business interests. These frescoes were what they saw every working day.

Nothing here is a saint, a miracle or a king. For a painting this large in the 1330s, that is astonishing. The subject is daily life, and the street is so busy that it helps to walk it from left to right, the way a visitor entering the room would.

lesson.title: Down the street
lesson.text: Three stops along the pavement, starting at the left edge.

spots.title: A wedding party
spots.text: A crowned bride in red rides a white horse, escorted by friends on foot and on horseback. A marriage means families trust the future enough to join their fortunes.

spots.title: The dancers
spots.text: Nine figures in patterned gowns wind hand in hand through the street while a tenth, at the left, sings and beats a tambourine. They pass under each other's raised arms.

spots.title: Open for business
spots.text: Under the arches, counters are set out. Shoes and stockings hang in one shop, and customers lean in. Trade happens in full view, with no guards in sight.

lesson.text: Did the dancers seem large to you? They are. Lorenzetti painted them noticeably bigger than the shoppers and riders beside them, which tells you they are not a report of something he saw. Dancing in the street was actually against Siena's rules. This ring of joined hands is a symbol: a city moving in step.
Lorenzetti argues with scenes instead of slogans. Peace is never written on the wall here; it is shown as people going about their day without fear.

A dance, a wedding and full shops all describe the present. A government also has to be judged on whether people invest in tomorrow. Lorenzetti found a sharp way to say that, and he put it far from the street, where you have to hunt for it.
This city is not finished. Somewhere, people are still building it. Can you find them?

spots.title: Builders on the roof
spots.text: Masons work on a scaffold against the dark blue sky. Some carry loads on their heads, others lay the wall. A city that keeps building is a city that expects to prosper.

lesson.text: Those workers stand at the very top of a hill of houses. Towers, balconies, loggias and tiled roofs are stacked one behind another, each seen from a slightly different angle. The rules of perspective, the geometry that makes a flat picture look deep, would not be worked out for another eighty years. Lorenzetti gets his depth by piling and overlapping.
Three lines show how he organized a whole town on a single wall.

lines.label: The street
lines.text: Almost every person stands below this line. People take the lower third of the wall, at the eye level of the men sitting in the room.

lines.label: The skyline
lines.text: Towers run all the way to the top edge, so there is hardly any sky. The city presses forward like a wall of its own, dense and solid.

lines.label: The city wall
lines.text: The notched brick wall slides down the right side and closes the town. Its gate stands open, and the fresco continues past it into farmland that this image does not show.

lesson.text: Beyond that wall, on the real fresco, the countryside rolls on for several more meters: fields, vineyards, hunters, farmers bringing goods to market. The whole wall is about 14 meters long (46 feet). It is often called the first great panoramic view of a real city and its land painted in Europe since ancient Rome.

The wall facing this one shows the same city under a tyrant: houses in ruins, soldiers in the streets, the only shop still open selling weapons. That fresco is far more damaged than this one, and large patches of its plaster are simply gone.

The town is recognizably Siena, not an imaginary anywhere. That matters, because the councillors were being shown their own streets and told: this is what you stand to keep or lose. With that in mind, wander through it yourself. Much of the pleasure is in the corners.

spots.title: Siena's cathedral
spots.text: In the top left corner, a black and white striped bell tower and a dome rise over the roofs. They belong to Siena's cathedral, the detail that tells every viewer which city this is.

spots.title: A lesson in progress
spots.text: Inside this arch, a teacher sits at a raised desk facing rows of listeners. Education has a place on the main street, right next to the shops.

spots.title: A birdcage
spots.text: A cage hangs in an upstairs window. It is a tiny domestic touch, the kind of thing people only bother with when they feel settled and safe.

spots.title: A rider seen from behind
spots.text: A horseman in a dark hat rides away from us, up a side street. Showing a figure from the back was a bold way to suggest that the town continues beyond what we can see.

spots.title: Goods arriving
spots.text: Pack animals loaded with bulky bales stand near the gate. Siena's wealth came from cloth and banking, and the bales are heading for the workshops.

spots.title: The countryside walks in
spots.text: A herdsman drives a tight flock of sheep toward the gate, and a woman behind him carries a basket on her head. Town and farmland depend on each other.

spots.title: Words for the rulers
spots.text: The painted band under the scene carries verses in Italian, not Latin, so that any citizen could read them. They open by telling those who govern to turn their eyes to the figure of Justice.

lesson.text: Ambrogio Lorenzetti disappears from the records in 1348, the year the Black Death reached Siena and killed perhaps half its people. He drew up his will that year and almost certainly died in the epidemic. The government of the Nine fell seven years later.

The councillors sat with this wall on one side and the ruined city on the other. Nobody in the room could look at one without knowing the other was behind them. Which raises a question the fresco leaves with you: if a painter were asked today to show your town well governed, what would he put in the street?

quiz.question: Where was this fresco painted?
options: In the meeting room of Siena's rulers
quiz.explanation: It covers the walls of the room in the Palazzo Pubblico where the Nine met.

quiz.question: Why are the dancers painted larger than the people around them?
options: They are a symbol of a city in harmony, not a street scene
They stand closer to the viewer
quiz.explanation: Their size marks them as a symbol; dancing in the street was in fact against the rules.

quiz.question: What are the figures on the rooftop doing?
quiz.explanation: Masons on a scaffold show a city confident enough to keep building.

quiz.question: What is fresco?
options: Oil paint on a wooden panel
Colored glass set in a wall
quiz.explanation: The color is brushed onto fresh plaster and dries into the wall.

quiz.question: What does the wall facing this one show?
options: The same city under a tyrant
quiz.explanation: It shows ruined houses and soldiers, the effects of bad government.

facts.text: The verses painted under the scene are written in Italian so that ordinary citizens could read them.
facts.explanation: They are in Italian, not Latin, and address those who govern.

facts.text: Lorenzetti used mathematical perspective with a single vanishing point to build his city.
facts.explanation: Perspective was worked out about eighty years later; he stacked and overlapped buildings instead.

facts.text: Each team of the Nine governed Siena for only two months.
facts.explanation: The councillors served short two-month terms and lived in the town hall while in office.
